in_text_mentions: Initial computed tomography (CT) of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) demonstrated a large perirenal fluid collection (6.9 × 6.8 × 6.6 cm) with an average attenuation of 52 Hounsfield units (HU). These hyperdense components, compared to the expected water density of simple urine (0-20 HU), are diagnostic of a hemorrhagic urinoma. The presence of fluid-fluid levels was seen, further corroborating the presence of blood products secondary to the calyceal rupture (Figure 1).

Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy to rule out myeloproliferative neoplasm showed normocellular marrow without evidence of myeloproliferative neoplasm. The bone marrow chromosome analysis was normal. Molecular tests for specific genetic mutations, including JAK2, CALR, BCR/ABL, and MPL were all negative. An abdominal ultrasound, performed due to a palpable abdominal mass, identified her severe left hydronephrosis (Figure 2A).

For her left hydronephrosis, a voiding cystourethrogram was performed to rule out vesicoureteral reflux, and it showed no abnormalities. To check renal function, serum creatinine was 0.6 mg/dL and BUN was 13 mg/dL. However, the renal MAG-3 scan (SignaTM Artist 1.5T, GE healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) demonstrated markedly impaired left renal function, making it difficult to assess for obstruction (Figure 2B). An abdominal MRI confirmed severe hydronephrosis with a paper-thin left renal cortex, suggesting ureteropelvic junction stenosis as the underlying cause (Figure 2C).

A: This axial CT scan of a 16-year-old girl shows a massive cystic mass (33-cm) arising from the retroperitoneum, which is the focus of the case report regarding a missed diagnosis of giant hydronephrosis. B: This coronal CT scan displays the same massive cystic retroperitoneal mass, relevant to the case of giant hydronephrosis being evaluated.
